subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Response]
passage:
Saturday night. At his college friend's wedding in Kolkata, after six months sober, Anirban drank whisky in the car park. He knew what he had done the moment he did it.
Sunday morning. His first thought was to hide it; nobody had seen. His second was his counsellor's line: secrets are where relapses grow. At 9 am he called Jeevan, his friend from the support group. "I drank last night. I'm telling you before I can talk myself out of it."
Jeevan was quiet a moment. "Thank you for calling. One night doesn't erase six months. Are you okay today? Let's get you to the Sunday meeting."
Tuesday. Anirban sat in Dr Sengupta's clinic and told the whole story. There was no lecture. They looked at what had led up to the car park, changed his plan for next month's wedding and booked a check-in for Friday. He walked out tired, but not ashamed enough to hide.

qa.q: Where did Anirban drink at the wedding?
Why did Anirban want to hide the lapse at first, and what made him tell someone?
qa.a: He first wanted to hide it because nobody had seen, but he remembered that secrets are where relapses grow and chose honesty over shame.

qa.q: What made the response to Anirban's lapse protective?
qa.a: Jeevan thanked him, said one night doesn't erase six months and got him to a meeting, and Dr Sengupta looked at triggers without a lecture, so shame didn't push him further.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have felt answering that 9 am call?
qa.a: Jeevan may have felt a jolt of worry, yet chose a calm, kind reply, knowing a punishing reaction could drive Anirban back into hiding.

grounding: Shows a lapse told quickly to a support person and a doctor, and kind, non-punishing reactions that keep a slip from becoming a full relapse.

subtype: Stage 8: Relapse as a setback, not the end [Response]
passage:
Pooja, you asked what to say when someone in the group admits a slip. Let me tell you about Irfan at twenty-five.
I had been off gambling for eleven months. Then a cricket final, a friend's phone, one bet. Then five. By midnight my month's savings were gone. I sat on the steps of our building in Bhopal and thought, That's it. Eleven months wasted. Might as well go all the way.
But I had promised my sponsor, Harish bhai, that I would call before I decided anything. So I called him at 1 am. He didn't shout. He said, "You rang me. That's the recovery working, beta. Come for chai at six."
And my Ammi, when I told her the next day, just put her hand on my head. No speech.
If either of them had shamed me that night, I don't think I'd be sitting here today as a counsellor. So when someone admits a slip, Pooja, thank them first.

qa.q: What did Harish bhai say when Irfan called at 1 am?
qa.a: "You rang me. That's the recovery working, beta. Come for chai at six."

qa.q: What was Irfan thinking on the building steps after the bets?
qa.a: Irfan felt the eleven months were wasted and thought of giving up completely, the pull that shame creates after a slip.

qa.q: What advice does Irfan give Pooja for when someone admits a slip, and why?
qa.a: Thank them first, because a kind, non-shaming reaction keeps the person connected to care instead of hiding.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt when Irfan told her the next day?
qa.a: Ammi was likely hurt and worried, yet she chose a silent hand on the head instead of a speech, offering comfort over blame.

grounding: Illustrates, through a counsellor's memory, telling a support person about a gambling lapse at once and the kind reactions that protected recovery.
